biblio-style: abbrvnat
abstract: "Nonlinear, non-Gaussian partially observed Markov process (POMP) models arise in various areas including epidemiology, ecology, and robotics. Model-based inferences typically involve computationally intensive Monte Carlo methods.  We introduce Pypomp, a Python library for data analysis via POMP models that uses JAX to take advantage of GPU hardware, automatic differentiation, and just-in-time compilation. By design, Pypomp supports model development and data analysis as well as method development, following the approach of the pomp R package. However, Pypomp obtains considerably higher performance: Pypomp running on one GPU can filter as many particles per second as 16,000 CPU cores running pomp. A central algorithm for Pypomp is the particle filter, and Pypomp is faster on our benchmark tests than other GPU-compatible particle filter libraries. The particle filter in Pypomp is differentiable, with a tunable bias-variance tradeoff."

```{python}
#| label: load-results
#| echo: false
#| warning: false  # pypomp_version's warnings go to the terminal, not the PDF
# Benchmark results come from the pypomp/quant submodule (article/quant),
# and the England and Wales measles fit from ../big_measles. Every number
# quoted in the text is computed here, so rerunning quant updates the paper.
import json
import math
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pypomp as pp
from IPython.display import Markdown
from packaging.version import Version

QUANT = Path("quant")
TIMING_MODELS = {
    "dacca": "Cholera, Dhaka",
    "measles": "Measles, London",
    "panel_measles": "Measles, 4-town panel",
    "spx": "S\\&P 500",
}


def load_timing(model):
    """Timings and run metadata for one quant timing test, keyed by backend."""
    out = {}
    for backend in ["R", "cpu", "gpu", "gpu_cute", "gpu_jax"]:
        d = QUANT / "tests" / model / "timing" / "results" / backend
        if d.is_dir():
            out[backend] = {
                "times": pd.read_csv(d / "timings.csv").set_index("phase")["time_seconds"],
                "meta": json.loads((d / "latest.json").read_text()),
            }
    return out


def pf_time(times):
    # pypomp's cold-start time includes JIT compilation; R has no warm-up.
    return times.get("pfilter_cold", times.get("pfilter_warm"))


def latex_table(cols, head, body):
    """A table at the text width, as raw LaTeX for a tbl- div.

    Pandoc writes Markdown tables as longtables, which can break across pages
    and then repeat the caption. cols is the tabular column spec, head the
    header lines (with their own row ends), and body the rows without them.
    """
    lines = [
        "\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{4pt}",
        f"\\begin{{tabular*}}{{\\linewidth}}{{@{{\\extracolsep{{\\fill}}}}{cols}@{{}}}}",
        "\\toprule", *head, "\\midrule",
        *[row + " \\\\" for row in body],
        "\\bottomrule", "\\end{tabular*}",
    ]
    return Markdown("```{=latex}\n" + "\n".join(lines) + "\n```")


timing = {m: load_timing(m) for m in TIMING_MODELS}
quant_sha = subprocess.run(
    ["git", "-C", str(QUANT), "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"],
    capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
).stdout.strip()

# Each table and figure states the Pypomp release behind it, which is checked
# across every quant job that went into it, so a partial rerun of quant can't
# silently mix releases. A mismatch, or a job with no recorded version,
# doesn't stop the render: it adds a red note to the caption (version_warning)
# and prints a warning to the terminal.
VERSION_WARNINGS = {}


def pypomp_version(item, jobs):
    """The Pypomp version for one table or figure, checked across its jobs.

    jobs is a list of (job, version) pairs, one for each quant run behind
    item, with version None if the run recorded none. If they all agree,
    return that version; otherwise, record a warning and return the range.
    """
    by_version = {}
    for job, v in jobs:
        by_version.setdefault(v, []).append(job)
    # Version handles release candidates such as 1.3.0rc1.
    recorded = sorted((v for v in by_version if v is not None), key=Version)
    if len(by_version) > 1 or not recorded:
        problem = "versions differ" if len(recorded) > 1 else "version not recorded"
        groups = "; ".join(
            f"{v or 'none'} for {', '.join(dict.fromkeys(by_version[v]))}"
            for v in [*recorded, None] if v in by_version
        ).removeprefix("none ")
        VERSION_WARNINGS[item] = f"Pypomp {problem}", groups
        # sys.__stderr__ reaches the terminal, and the chunk's warning: false
        # keeps it out of the PDF.
        print(f"WARNING: {item}: Pypomp {problem}: {groups}", file=sys.__stderr__)
    if not recorded:
        return "(version not recorded)"
    return recorded[0] if len(recorded) == 1 else f"{recorded[0]}--{recorded[-1]}"


def version_warning(item):
    """A red note for item's caption if its Pypomp version check failed."""
    if item not in VERSION_WARNINGS:
        return Markdown("<!-- -->")  # an empty result would print the inline code
    problem, groups = VERSION_WARNINGS[item]
    groups = groups.replace("_", "\\_")
    return Markdown(f"\\textcolor{{red}}{{\\textbf{{{problem}:}} {groups}.}}")


def timing_jobs(backends):
    """(job, Pypomp version) for each quant timing run with these backends."""
    return [
        (f"{m}/timing/{b}", t[b]["meta"].get("pypomp_version"))
        for m, t in timing.items() for b in backends if b in t
    ]


tbl_timing_full_version = pypomp_version("tbl-timing-full", timing_jobs(["cpu", "gpu", "gpu_cute"]))
# Appendix -@sec-samplers compares IF2 and PF for the London measles model
# with jax.random and pypomp.random samplers; only the warning is used.
pypomp_version(
    "jax-samplers", [j for j in timing_jobs(["gpu", "gpu_jax"]) if j[0].startswith("measles/")]
)
pomp_bench_version = timing["dacca"]["R"]["meta"]["pomp_version"]
panelpomp_bench_version = timing["dacca"]["R"]["meta"]["panelPomp_version"]
r_bench_version = timing["dacca"]["R"]["meta"]["r_version"]
gpu_name = timing["dacca"]["gpu"]["meta"]["slurm"]["gpu_type"].replace("NVIDIA ", "")
# R and Pypomp CPU runs used 36-core nodes, not all with the same processor.
cpu_models = sorted({
    r["meta"]["hardware"]["cpu_model"].replace("Intel(R) Xeon(R) ", "").split(" CPU")[0]
    for t in timing.values() for b, r in t.items() if b in ("R", "cpu")
})
# The tables put the default (XLA) and CuTe GPU runs side by side, so check
# that they used the same GPU model, and that CuTe used Philox. (Their Pypomp
# versions are checked by pypomp_version.)
for m, t in timing.items():
    xla, cute = t["gpu"]["meta"], t["gpu_cute"]["meta"]
    assert xla["backend"] == "default" and (cute["backend"], cute["cute_rng"]) == ("cute", "philox"), m
    assert {d["slurm"]["gpu_type"] for d in [xla, cute]} == {"NVIDIA " + gpu_name}, m

# The R scripts run one doParallel worker per core on a 36-core node, and each
# phase splits independent searches or filters evenly across the workers, so
# one core would take R_CORES times as long. (latest.json's slurm.cpus is
# cpus-per-task, which is 1, not the number of workers.)
R_CORES = 36
mif_speedups = [
    t["R"]["times"]["mif"] / t["gpu"]["times"]["mif"] for t in timing.values()
]
mif_core_ratios = [R_CORES * s for s in mif_speedups]
# At the benchmark sizes, CuTe's longer compilation can outweigh its faster IF2
# iterations. The text names the models where CuTe's IF2 was slower than XLA's.
cute_slower_mif = [
    m for m, t in timing.items() if t["gpu_cute"]["times"]["mif"] > t["gpu"]["times"]["mif"]
]
assert cute_slower_mif == ["dacca", "measles", "panel_measles"], cute_slower_mif
# The text says the panel's XLA IF2 ratio of R time to GPU time is below London's.
assert mif_speedups[list(timing).index("panel_measles")] < mif_speedups[list(timing).index("measles")]


def fmt_ratio(x):
    return f"{x:.1f}" if x < 10 else f"{x:.0f}"


# Split R time / GPU time into software (R / Pypomp on 36-core CPU nodes) and
# hardware (Pypomp CPU / Pypomp GPU), over the IF2 and PF rows of
# @tbl-timing-full that have a Pypomp CPU run.
software_ratios, hardware_ratios = [], []
for t in timing.values():
    if "cpu" in t:
        for get in [lambda s: s["mif"], pf_time]:
            r, py_cpu, gpu = (get(t[b]["times"]) for b in ["R", "cpu", "gpu"])
            software_ratios.append(r / py_cpu)
            hardware_ratios.append(py_cpu / gpu)

# GPU scaling tests: more chains at J = 1,000, or more particles per chain at a
# fixed number of chains. Each configuration ran in its own process with XLA
# preallocation off, so peak_vram_mb is the memory it actually used. IF2 ran
# twice with the same short M: the first run includes JIT compilation and the
# second does not. Project each configuration to the benchmark's IF2 length,
# compilation included, to compare with @tbl-timing.
def r_mif_config(model):
    """Particles per IF2 chain and IF2 iterations in the R timing run."""
    cfg = timing[model]["R"]["meta"]["run_config"]
    if model == "spx":
        return cfg["Np"], cfg["Nmif"]
    if model == "panel_measles":
        return cfg["NP_FITR"], cfg["NFITR"]
    return cfg["NP"], cfg["NFITR"]


def scaling_r_cores(model, backend="gpu"):
    s = pd.read_csv(QUANT / "tests" / model / "scaling/results" / backend / "scaling.csv")
    np_r, nfitr = r_mif_config(model)
    # In the R timing run, each core ran one IF2 chain (over every unit of a panel).
    r_core_rate = np_r * nfitr / timing[model]["R"]["times"]["mif"]
    compile_s = s["mif_cold_seconds"] - s["mif_warm_seconds"]
    mif_s = compile_s + nfitr * s["mif_per_iter_seconds"]
    s["r_cores"] = s["total_particles_mif"] * nfitr / mif_s / r_core_rate
    return s


SCALING_MODELS = ["dacca", "measles", "panel_measles", "spx"]
scaling = {m: scaling_r_cores(m) for m in SCALING_MODELS}
peak_r_cores = {m: s["r_cores"].max() for m, s in scaling.items()}
peak_gain = {m: peak_r_cores[m] / c for m, c in zip(timing, mif_core_ratios)}

# The same scaling grids with Pypomp's optional CuTe backend and its Philox
# random number generator (quant's gpu_cute jobs), on the same GPU model.
scaling_meta = {
    (m, b): json.loads((QUANT / "tests" / m / "scaling/results" / b / "latest.json").read_text())
    for m in SCALING_MODELS for b in ["gpu", "gpu_cute"]
}
cute_meta = {m: scaling_meta[m, "gpu_cute"] for m in SCALING_MODELS}
assert all(
    d["backend"] == "cute" and d["cute_rng"] == "philox"
    and d["slurm"]["gpu_type"].replace("NVIDIA ", "") == gpu_name
    for d in cute_meta.values()
), cute_meta
scaling_jobs = [(f"{m}/scaling/{b}", d.get("pypomp_version")) for (m, b), d in scaling_meta.items()]
# The peak columns of @tbl-timing come from the scaling tests, and
# @fig-scaling marks the XLA benchmark of @tbl-timing.
tbl_timing_version = pypomp_version("tbl-timing", timing_jobs(["gpu", "gpu_cute"]) + scaling_jobs)
fig_scaling_version = pypomp_version("fig-scaling", scaling_jobs + timing_jobs(["gpu"]))
scaling_cute = {m: scaling_r_cores(m, "gpu_cute") for m in SCALING_MODELS}
peak_r_cores_cute = {m: s["r_cores"].max() for m, s in scaling_cute.items()}
# The text says CuTe's throughput for the S&P 500 model peaked before the
# largest configuration of each scaling branch and then fell, and that for the
# other models it changed by less than CUTE_TAIL over the last doubling of
# particles, so their peaks are close to what these configurations can reach.
CUTE_TAIL = 0.03
for m, s in scaling_cute.items():
    for kind, g in s.groupby("scaling_type"):
        g = g.sort_values("total_particles_mif")
        if m == "spx":
            assert g["r_cores"].idxmax() != g.index[-1], (m, kind)
            continue
        last, prev = g.iloc[-1], g.iloc[-2]
        assert last["total_particles_mif"] == 2 * prev["total_particles_mif"], (m, kind)
        assert abs(last["r_cores"] / prev["r_cores"] - 1) < CUTE_TAIL, (m, kind)
spx_cute = scaling_cute["spx"]
spx_cute_peak_at = {  # millions of particles at the CuTe peak of each branch
    kind: g.loc[g["r_cores"].idxmax(), "total_particles_mif"] / 1e6
    for kind, g in spx_cute.groupby("scaling_type")
}
# The abstract, which can't run code, quotes the CuTe peak as 16,000 cores.
assert math.floor(max(peak_r_cores_cute.values()) / 1000) == 16, peak_r_cores_cute


def compile_range(scalings):
    """Smallest and largest IF2 compilation time, in seconds, across scaling runs."""
    c = pd.concat([s["mif_cold_seconds"] - s["mif_warm_seconds"] for s in scalings.values()])
    return c.min(), c.max()


xla_compile_s, cute_compile_s = compile_range(scaling), compile_range(scaling_cute)


def bench_particles(model):
    """Total particles in flight during IF2 in the @tbl-timing benchmark."""
    cfg = timing[model]["R"]["meta"]["run_config"]
    return cfg.get("NSTARTS", cfg.get("Nstarts")) * r_mif_config(model)[0]


bench_totals = [bench_particles(m) for m in SCALING_MODELS]
peak_totals = [
    s.loc[s["r_cores"].idxmax(), "total_particles_mif"] for s in scaling.values()
]

spx_scaling = scaling["spx"]
spx_n_obs = len(pp.models.spx().ys)
n_dacca_obs = len(pp.models.dacca().ys)


# The two scaling branches were run on different grids of total particles, so
# compare them by interpolating each onto the range where they overlap.
def spx_throughput_at(kind, totals):
    s = spx_scaling[spx_scaling["scaling_type"] == kind].sort_values("total_particles_mif")
    return np.interp(np.log(totals), np.log(s["total_particles_mif"]), s["r_cores"])


spx_totals = spx_scaling.groupby("scaling_type")["total_particles_mif"]
spx_overlap = np.exp(np.linspace(
    np.log(spx_totals.min().max()), np.log(spx_totals.max().min()), 25
))
spx_chain_advantage = np.mean(
    spx_throughput_at("chains", spx_overlap) / spx_throughput_at("particles", spx_overlap)
)

# GPU memory per particle: the slope of peak memory against total particles,
# in MB per million particles (bytes per particle). Small configurations sit on
# the allocator's 64-256 MB steps, so fit each model's CuTe configurations with
# at least VRAM_FIT_MIN million particles, pooling both ways of adding
# particles. XLA's grids stop at a few million particles, too few for a slope.
VRAM_FIT_MIN = 4


def vram_slope(s):
    s = s[s["total_particles_mif"] >= VRAM_FIT_MIN * 1e6]
    return np.polyfit(s["total_particles_mif"] / 1e6, s["peak_vram_mb"], 1)[0]


vram_per_m = {m: vram_slope(scaling_cute[m]) for m in SCALING_MODELS}
# The text says memory per particle doesn't depend on how particles were added
# (each branch's slope is within 10% of the pooled one), and that at the largest
# XLA configuration of each branch, XLA used within 10% of CuTe's memory.
for m in SCALING_MODELS:
    for kind, g in scaling_cute[m].groupby("scaling_type"):
        assert abs(vram_slope(g) / vram_per_m[m] - 1) < 0.1, (m, kind, vram_slope(g))
        x = scaling[m][scaling[m]["scaling_type"] == kind]
        x = x.loc[x["total_particles_mif"].idxmax()]
        c = g[g["total_particles_mif"] == x["total_particles_mif"]]["peak_vram_mb"]
        assert len(c) == 1 and abs(x["peak_vram_mb"] / c.iloc[0] - 1) < 0.1, (m, kind)

jax_sampler_slowdown = (
    timing["measles"]["gpu_jax"]["times"]["mif"] / timing["measles"]["gpu"]["times"]["mif"]
)
jax_sampler_pf_slowdown = (
    pf_time(timing["measles"]["gpu_jax"]["times"]) / pf_time(timing["measles"]["gpu"]["times"])
)
SAMPLERS = json.loads((QUANT / "tests/samplers/benchmark_results.json").read_text())
SAMPLER_ROWS = {  # distribution: label, cached regime with parameters across the switches
    "poisson": ("Poisson", "Mixed Rates (around switches)"),
    "binomial": ("Binomial", "Mixed Grid (around switches)"),
    "gamma": ("Gamma", "Mixed Shapes (around switch)"),
    "nbinomial": ("Negative binomial", "Mixed Grid (around switches)"),
}
max_w1_norm = max(max(g["w_dist_norm"]) for g in SAMPLERS["grids"].values())
# GPU speedup of pypomp.random over jax.random, for distributions jax.random has.
sampler_gpu_speedups = [
    t["t_jax_gpu"] / t["t_pp_gpu"]
    for t in (SAMPLERS[d][regime] for d, (_, regime) in SAMPLER_ROWS.items())
    if t.get("t_jax_gpu") is not None
]
# benchmark_results.json gathers the GPU and CPU timing jobs and the W1 grids.
# quant's sampler test doesn't record their Pypomp versions yet; the ms reads
# them from "pypomp_versions": {"gpu": ..., "cpu": ..., "grids": ...}.
tbl_samplers_version = pypomp_version("tbl-samplers", [
    (f"samplers/{job}", SAMPLERS.get("pypomp_versions", {}).get(job))
    for job in ["gpu", "cpu", "grids"]
])

# England and Wales measles fit (all 1,422 towns) on one GPU with the CuTe
# backend and its Philox random number generator (quant
# tests/panel_measles/big_timing).
BIG = QUANT / "tests/panel_measles/big_timing/results/gpu_cute"
big_meta = json.loads((BIG / "latest_rl4.json").read_text())
assert big_meta["backend"] == "cute" and big_meta["cute_rng"] == "philox", big_meta
big_par = {k.lower(): v for k, v in big_meta["run_config"].items()}
assert big_par["run_level"] == 4, big_par
tbl_big_measles_version = pypomp_version(
    "tbl-big-measles", [("panel_measles/big_timing/gpu_cute", big_meta.get("pypomp_version"))]
)
# Wall-clock seconds for each method call. The total leaves out building the
# model and mixing and matching, which take a few minutes together.
big_mif_s = big_meta["stage_wall_s"]["mif"]
big_pf1_s = big_meta["stage_wall_s"]["pfilter_eval1"]
big_pf2_s = big_meta["stage_wall_s"]["pfilter_final"]
big_total_s = big_mif_s + big_pf1_s + big_pf2_s

# R estimate, extrapolated from panelPomp's cost on the 4-town panel in quant,
# which covers the same 1950-1963 period with the same daily Euler steps. Cost
# is assumed linear in particles, IF2 iterations and towns. In the quant run,
# each of the 36 cores ran one IF2 chain and then NSTARTS * NREPS_EVAL / 36
# particle filters.
panel_R = timing["panel_measles"]["R"]
panel_cfg = panel_R["meta"]["run_config"]
n_small = len(panel_cfg["units"])
r_mif_cost = panel_R["times"]["mif"] / (panel_cfg["NP_FITR"] * panel_cfg["NFITR"] * n_small)
pf_per_core = panel_cfg["NSTARTS"] * panel_cfg["NREPS_EVAL"] / R_CORES
r_pf_cost = panel_R["times"]["pfilter_warm"] / (pf_per_core * panel_cfg["NP_EVAL"] * n_small)

n_big = big_par["n_units"]
# IF2 chains are sequential, so R gains nothing from more cores than chains.
r_big_mif_s = r_mif_cost * big_par["np_fitr"] * big_par["nfitr"] * n_big
r_one_pf_s = r_pf_cost * big_par["np_eval"] * n_big
r_big_pf1_s = math.ceil(big_par["nreps_fitr"] * big_par["nreps_eval"] / R_CORES) * r_one_pf_s
r_big_pf2_s = math.ceil(big_par["nreps_eval"] / R_CORES) * r_one_pf_s
r_big_total_s = r_big_mif_s + r_big_pf1_s + r_big_pf2_s
# On one core, every IF2 chain and particle filter runs in turn.
n_big_pf = big_par["nreps_fitr"] * big_par["nreps_eval"] + big_par["nreps_eval"]
r_big_1core_s = big_par["nreps_fitr"] * r_big_mif_s + n_big_pf * r_one_pf_s

# The particle filter workloads of @tbl-timing-full in other Python libraries
# (quant tests/library_comparison), rerun on the same GPU model as @tbl-timing.
# first_s is the first call, including JIT compilation, and warm_s a later
# call; status "timeout" means the run was stopped at first_s seconds, and
# "projected" means one CPU filter's time times the number of filters, divided
# by 36 cores. The CPU-only libraries were not rerun, and their versions are
# recorded only in the original RTX 3090 table.
LIB_DIR = QUANT / "tests/library_comparison"
lib_times = pd.read_csv(LIB_DIR / "table_rtxpro6000.csv").set_index(["model", "column"])
lib_version = (
    pd.concat([lib_times, pd.read_csv(LIB_DIR / "table.csv").set_index(["model", "column"])])
    ["version"].dropna().groupby(level="column").first()
)
GPU_LIBS = ["pfjax", "cuthbert", "pydpf"]
CPU_LIBS = ["particles", "pypfilt"]
# Pypomp's column "pypomp_cute" ran with set_backend("cute", rng="philox"),
# with all filters in one batch, as the other GPU libraries' adapters run them.
for m in TIMING_MODELS:
    for line in (LIB_DIR / m / "results/gpu_rtxpro6000/results_pypomp_cute.jsonl").open():
        r = json.loads(line)
        assert (r["backend"], r["cute_rng"]) == ("cute", "philox"), (m, r["backend"], r["cute_rng"])
# How many times faster Pypomp's compiled filter ran with CuTe than with XLA.
lib_cute_gain = [
    lib_times.loc[(m, "pypomp"), "warm_s"] / lib_times.loc[(m, "pypomp_cute"), "warm_s"]
    for m in TIMING_MODELS
]
# Check the version of every Pypomp run in the GPU results directories, not
# the single version per library that make_tables.py writes to the table.
tbl_libraries_version = pypomp_version("tbl-libraries", [
    (f"library_comparison/{m}/{r['backend']}", r.get("versions", {}).get("pypomp"))
    for m in TIMING_MODELS
    for f in ["results.jsonl", "results_pypomp_cute.jsonl"]
    for r in map(json.loads, (LIB_DIR / m / "results/gpu_rtxpro6000" / f).open())
    if r.get("lib") == "pypomp"  # records of failed runs have no "lib"
])
# The text says whether the library comparison used the release in @tbl-timing-full.
lib_release_text = (
    "the same Pypomp release" if tbl_libraries_version == tbl_timing_full_version
    else f"Pypomp {tbl_libraries_version} rather than {tbl_timing_full_version}"
)


def lib_s(model, lib, col="first_s"):
    return lib_times.loc[(model, lib), col]


def lib_ratio(model, lib):
    """The other library's compiled (warm) time divided by Pypomp's."""
    return lib_s(model, lib, "warm_s") / lib_s(model, "pypomp", "warm_s")


def fmt_range(xs, digits):
    """'a to b' for a range of ratios, or 'about a' when both round the same."""
    lo, hi = f"{min(xs):.{digits}f}", f"{max(xs):.{digits}f}"
    return f"about {lo}" if lo == hi else f"{lo} to {hi}"


# jax.random-based libraries on the London measles model, relative to Pypomp.
lib_measles_jax = [lib_ratio("measles", l) for l in ["pfjax", "cuthbert"]]
lib_pydpf = [lib_ratio(m, "pydpf") for m in ["dacca", "measles", "panel_measles"]]
lib_dacca_jax = [lib_ratio("dacca", l) for l in ["pfjax", "cuthbert"]]
# The text says Pypomp's compiled filter is the fastest GPU library on every
# model (a timed-out run has no warm time, so it compares as not faster), and
# that pydpf's first call on the S&P 500 model is the only one faster than
# Pypomp's, with every GPU library's first call there under two seconds.
for m in TIMING_MODELS:
    assert not any(
        lib_s(m, l, "warm_s") <= lib_s(m, "pypomp", "warm_s") for l in GPU_LIBS
    ), m
    faster = [l for l in GPU_LIBS if lib_s(m, l) < lib_s(m, "pypomp")]
    assert faster == (["pydpf"] if m == "spx" else []), (m, faster)
assert all(lib_s("spx", l) < 2 for l in ["pypomp", *GPU_LIBS])
# CPU-only libraries relative to the measured pomp (or panelPomp) time.
lib_cpu_vs_r = {
    l: [lib_s(m, l) / pf_time(timing[m]["R"]["times"]) for m in TIMING_MODELS]
    for l in CPU_LIBS
}

HOUR, DAY = 3600, 86400
big_hours = f"{big_total_s / HOUR:.0f}"
r_big_months = f"{r_big_total_s / (30.44 * DAY):.1f}"
big_speedup = f"{r_big_total_s / big_total_s:.0f}"
r_big_1core_years = f"{r_big_1core_s / (365.25 * DAY):.1f}"
big_core_ratio = f"{r_big_1core_s / big_total_s:,.0f}"
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}
Partially observed Markov process (POMP) models provide a flexible framework for modeling dynamic systems whose underlying state is not directly observed.
POMP models, also known as state-space models or hidden Markov models, consist of a latent Markov process and incomplete or noisy observations.
The task of evaluating the likelihood function and estimating latent states for a POMP model is called the filtering problem. 

Pypomp is a Python library combining advances in hardware, software, and algorithms for POMP models, with an emphasis on inference via the particle filter (PF).
PF, also known as sequential Monte Carlo, provides an estimate of the likelihood of a POMP model [@arulampalam02].
The basic PF algorithm needs to simulate from the process model but does not evaluate its transition probabilities, a property known as plug-and-play (P&P) [@breto09].
Pypomp focuses on P&P methods because they facilitate scientific modeling, enabling applications in epidemiology [@mietchen24; @fox22; @wen24], ecology [@augermethe21; @marino19; @blackwood13], finance [@breto14], robotics [@jonschkowski18] and other domains where nonlinear mechanistic stochastic dynamic models are pertinent.
Pypomp provides P&P inference methods extending PF: maximum likelihood parameter estimation by iterated filtering (IF2) [@ionides15], Bayesian inference by particle Markov chain Monte Carlo [@andrieu10], and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) via a differentiable particle filter (DPF) algorithm called a measurement-off-parameter (MOP) particle filter [@tan24].

Pypomp provides a framework for specifying models and inference methods, a range of pre-built models and methods, and various graphical and diagnostic tools to assist practical data analysis.
Thus, Pypomp supports complete data analysis workflows, facilitating the evaluation of a range of models and statistical methods.
Models and methods share an interface so that new models can readily be tested on pre-existing methods, and new methods can be tested on pre-existing models.
These design features are inherited from the R package pomp [@king16].
Although the method interface of Pypomp (and pomp) is not limited to P&P algorithms, experience has shown that P&P approaches are convenient for scientific data analysis.
Theoretical obstacles have limited the practical scope of non-P&P algorithms [@roberts01; @karppinen24].

Pypomp leverages JAX [@bradbury18] to provide just-in-time (JIT) compilation, automatic differentiation (AD), and the capability to run on massively parallel hardware such as GPUs.
When the state space is small and discrete, or sufficiently close to linear Gaussian for applicability of the extended or unscented Kalman filter, the Dynamax library [@linderman25] provides JAX-based solutions.
Other JAX-based libraries providing PF and DPF methods for POMP models include PFJAX [@lysy22] and Cuthbert [@duffield26].
PyDPF [@brady26] provides a DPF using PyTorch and focuses on POMP models parameterized using neural networks.
The NumPy-based libraries particles [@chopin20], a general sequential Monte Carlo framework, and pypfilt [@moss24] provide PF without AD.
Pypomp distinguishes itself from these other packages by (i) following the design decisions of pomp that support a full data analysis workflow; (ii) superior performance on benchmark tests.
Pypomp is not limited to PF methods, and includes, for example, the approximate Bayesian computing (ABC) P&P algorithm of @marjoram03.
However, PF has proved an effective tool for the development and analysis of POMP models in scientific contexts.

Pypomp compiles models with JAX's XLA compiler by default; on NVIDIA GPUs, an optional CuTe backend translates them into CUDA kernels [@thakkar23; @cecka26].
With enough particles and method replications, one GPU running the CuTe backend runs iterated filtering as fast as `{python} f"{min(peak_r_cores_cute.values()):,.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(peak_r_cores_cute.values()):,.0f}"` CPU cores running pomp (Appendix -@sec-scaling).
Such replications are routine in practice: practical likelihood maximization involves searching from many initial parameter vectors, and Monte Carlo adjusted profile (MCAP) confidence intervals [@ionides17], implemented in Pypomp as `mcap`, require maximizations.
Profile likelihood approaches have been found preferable to Fisher information for confidence interval construction for linear Gaussian POMP models [@wheeler25arma].
MCAP algorithms can lead to efficient inference even in a limit where the Monte Carlo error grows with the amount of data [@ning21].

Algorithms to take advantage of JIT, AD, and GPU are an area of active development.
Pypomp implements the MOP P&P DPF algorithm of @tan24, with the resulting derivative being called DMOP implemented within the `train` method.
DMOP is competitive on benchmark problems when combined with Adam SGD, especially when using IF2 for a warm start [@tan24].
Pypomp provides inverse transform sampling methods for use in `rproc` and `rmeas` since the rejection sampling used in some `jax.random` samplers is inefficient on GPUs [@giles16; @giles24; @temme92].
These samplers run `{python} f"{min(sampler_gpu_speedups):.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(sampler_gpu_speedups):.0f}"` times faster than `jax.random` on a GPU.
Quantiles of inverse and rejection sampling draws differ by at most `{python} f"{max_w1_norm * 100:.1f}"`% of a standard deviation on average (Appendix -@sec-samplers).

# POMP Modeling in Pypomp {#sec-pomp}

Let $\{X(t), t_0 \leq t \leq t_{N}\}$ denote the latent process, and write $Y_{1:N}$ for the measurement process at times $t_{1:N}$.
We suppose $Y_n$ is conditionally independent of the other latent states and measurements given $X_n=X(t_n)$.
The data are observed values, $y^*_{1:N}$.
A POMP model is specified by its initial state distribution, $f_{X_0}(x_0 ; \theta)$, state transition density $f_{X_{n+1}|X_{n}}(x_{n+1} | x_{n} ; \theta)$, and measurement density $f_{Y_n|X_n}(y_n| x_n; \theta)$, where $\theta$ denotes a vector of model parameters.
For P\&P methods, it suffices to specify a simulator for $f_{X_0}(x_0 ; \theta)$ known as \texttt{rinit}, a simulator for $f_{X_{n+1}|X_{n}}(x_{n+1} | x_{n} ; \theta)$ known as \texttt{rproc}, a simulator for $f_{Y_n|X_n}(y_n| x_n; \theta)$ known as \texttt{rmeas}, and an evaluator for $f_{Y_n|X_n}(y_n| x_n; \theta)$ known as \texttt{dmeas}.
The user passes JAX-compatible code for these functions, together with the data, to build a \texttt{Pomp} class model object using the \texttt{Pomp} constructor function.
Tutorials are available at [https://github.com/pypomp/tutorials](https://github.com/pypomp/tutorials).
Pypomp includes models for historical monthly cholera mortality in Dhaka, Bangladesh (`pypomp.models.dacca`), historical weekly measles cases in London, UK (`pypomp.models.measles.pomp`), daily log returns of the S&P 500 index (`pypomp.models.spx`), and a panel model for measles cases in up to 1,422 urban and rural districts in England and Wales (`pypomp.models.measles.panel_pomp`).

A collection of POMP models is a PanelPOMP [@breto20], and each constituent POMP is called a _unit_.
Parameters may be unit-specific or shared between units.
Marginalized panel iterated filtering (MPIF) [@wheeler25] and DMOP provide likelihood maximization for models of class `PanelPomp`.

Below, we demonstrate maximum likelihood estimation with IF2 (`mif`) followed by refinement using SGD (`train`) and then log-likelihood evaluation using PF (`pfilter`), on the `spx` model.
Each method stores its convergence records, execution time, and arguments in the `results_history` attribute of the `Pomp` object, enabling sequential method chaining and diagnostic investigation by helper methods such as `traces`. 
```{python}
# | label: spx-inference-workflow
# | echo: true
# | cache: true
import pypomp as pp, jax
spx_obj = pp.models.spx()
spx_obj.mif(J=1000, M=10, key=jax.random.key(1), rw_sd=pp.RWSigma(
    sigmas={"mu": 0.02, "kappa": 0.02, "theta": 0.02,
            "xi": 0.02, "rho": 0.02, "V_0": 0.1},
    init_names=["V_0"]).geometric_cooling(a=0.5))
spx_obj.train(J=1000, M=10, optimizer=pp.Adam(), eta=pp.LearningRate(
    {name: 0.001 for name in spx_obj.canonical_param_names}
    ).geometric_decay(decay_rate=0.5, M=10))
spx_obj.pfilter(J=1000, reps=10) 
```


Two performance questions are: (i) what is the benefit of using GPU hardware versus CPU? (ii) how does Pypomp compare in speed to alternative GPU-based particle filter libraries? 
To address (i), we compare Pypomp on a GPU with pomp on a CPU because that informs a natural decision for scientists considering Pypomp as a data analysis tool. 
With model code in compiled C snippets, pomp has comparable speed to other high-performance CPU-based packages for POMP models [@fitzjohn20]. 
@tbl-timing shows four models with different characteristics (details in Appendix -@sec-benchmarks and <https://github.com/pypomp/quant>).
Efficiency peaks when the GPU is saturated, and for small tasks CuTe's longer compilation can outweigh its faster iterations (Appendix -@sec-scaling).
With `jax.random` samplers instead of `pypomp.random`, IF2 for the London measles model took `{python} f"{jax_sampler_slowdown:.0f}"` times longer (Appendix -@sec-samplers).
To address (ii), Appendix -@sec-libraries runs the same particle filter workloads in five other Python libraries; on the London measles model, once compiled, `pfjax` and `cuthbert` took `{python} fmt_range(lib_measles_jax, 0)` times as long as Pypomp.

# Full benchmark results {#sec-benchmarks}

The four benchmark models stress different parts of the particle filter, which helps locate performance bottlenecks.

**Cholera, Dhaka.**
The cholera model of @king08 has `{python} f"{n_dacca_obs:,}"` monthly observations with 20 Euler steps between each, and each step updates a stochastic differential equation with one normal draw.
The process model is cheap, but there are many steps between resamples, so this model isolates the per-step overhead inside the process model.

**Measles, London.**
The measles model of @he10 has weekly case reports from 1950 to 1963 and takes a daily Euler step, interpolating covariates and drawing binomial, gamma, and Poisson random variables at every step.
It has a relatively expensive process model, so it isolates how the GPU handles heavy computation per particle, while testing the fast samplers in `pypomp.random` (Appendix -@sec-samplers).

**Measles, 4-town panel.**
The panel model fits the same measles model to `{python} ", ".join(panel_cfg["units"][:-1])`, and `{python} panel_cfg["units"][-1]` jointly, with some parameters shared across towns and the rest specific to each town.
MPIF [@wheeler25] filters the towns sequentially within each iteration, so an iteration costs about four single-town iterations with the same number of particles in flight.
This model tests the panel methods used in Appendix -@sec-big-measles-details.
With the default XLA backend, its IF2 ratio of R pomp CPU time to GPU time is lower than for the London model because R runs it relatively fast, likely because the random variate generators in R can take a cheaper route for the smaller parameter values of the smaller towns.

**S&P 500.**
The stochastic volatility model of @breto14 has `{python} f"{spx_n_obs:,}"` daily log returns and takes one step of its process model per observation, with a single normal draw.
Each step between resamples is very cheap, so fixed per-observation costs such as resampling can dominate.

```{python}
#| echo: false

def bench_workload(model):
    """IF2 particles, iterations, and searches, and PF replicates per parameter set.

    The quant scripts name these settings differently for each model and
    language, so read them from every backend's run and check that they agree.
    """
    workloads = set()
    for run in timing[model].values():
        cfg = {k.upper(): v for k, v in run["meta"]["run_config"].items()}
        np_fitr = cfg.get("NP_FITR", cfg.get("NP"))
        # Every benchmark filters with as many particles as IF2 uses.
        assert cfg.get("NP_EVAL", np_fitr) == np_fitr, model
        workloads.add((
            np_fitr,
            cfg.get("NFITR", cfg.get("NMIF")),
            cfg["NSTARTS"],
            cfg.get("NREPS_EVAL", cfg.get("NREPS")),
        ))
    assert len(workloads) == 1, (model, workloads)
    return workloads.pop()


workload = {m: bench_workload(m) for m in TIMING_MODELS}
# The text below describes the cholera and both measles benchmarks together.
assert workload["dacca"] == workload["measles"] == workload["panel_measles"], workload
assert workload["spx"][2] == workload["dacca"][2], workload
wl_np, wl_nfitr, wl_nstarts, wl_nreps = workload["dacca"]
spx_np, spx_nfitr, _, spx_nreps = workload["spx"]
```

@tbl-timing benchmarks Pypomp `{python} tbl_timing_full_version` against pomp `{python} pomp_bench_version` and panelPomp `{python} panelpomp_bench_version`.
R pomp and Pypomp run the same workload in a given benchmark.
CPU runs used 36-core nodes with Intel Xeon `{python} " or ".join(cpu_models)` processors, and GPU runs used one NVIDIA `{python} gpu_name`.
Each benchmark runs `{python} wl_nstarts` IF2 searches from the same starting points and then runs replicate particle filters at each search's IF2 estimate, with as many particles per filter as per search.
The cholera and both measles benchmarks use `{python} f"{wl_np:,}"` particles, `{python} wl_nfitr` IF2 iterations, and `{python} wl_nreps` particle filter replicates, and the S&P 500 benchmark uses `{python} f"{spx_np:,}"` particles, `{python} spx_nfitr` iterations, and `{python} spx_nreps` replicates.

Fitting the measles model of @he10 to all `{python} f"{n_big:,}"` towns and cities for 1950--1963 took one GPU running the CuTe backend `{python} big_hours` hours, including likelihood evaluation, versus an estimated `{python} r_big_months` months for R on a 36-core node, extrapolating linearly from panelPomp's cost on the 4-town panel (Appendix -@sec-big-measles-details).
Thus, Pypomp enables a scientific analysis that was previously considered infeasible [@becker17].

@tbl-timing-full extends @tbl-timing with IF2 and particle filter times for Pypomp on a 36-core CPU node like those used for R pomp.
Pypomp on CPU was `{python} fmt_ratio(min(software_ratios))` to `{python} fmt_ratio(max(software_ratios))` times faster than R pomp, and moving Pypomp to the GPU with the default XLA backend makes it another `{python} fmt_ratio(min(hardware_ratios))` to `{python} fmt_ratio(max(hardware_ratios))` times faster.
These workloads are sized for R and too small to saturate the GPU, so the GPU ratios understate what the GPU can do.
At these sizes, the CuTe backend's longer compilation outweighs its faster iterations: its IF2 was slower than XLA's for every model except the S&P 500.
At its peak throughput in the scaling tests (Appendix -@sec-scaling), one GPU runs IF2 `{python} f"{min(peak_r_cores.values()) / R_CORES:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(peak_r_cores.values()) / R_CORES:.0f}"` times as fast as R on the 36-core node with the default XLA backend, and `{python} f"{min(peak_r_cores_cute.values()) / R_CORES:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(peak_r_cores_cute.values()) / R_CORES:.0f}"` times as fast with the CuTe backend.

::: {#tbl-timing-full}

# Comparison with other particle filter libraries {#sec-libraries}

@tbl-libraries times the particle filter workloads of @tbl-timing-full in other Python particle filter libraries, with each model written as a user of that library would write it.
Every library runs the bootstrap particle filter with the same number of filters and particles as in @tbl-timing-full.
The GPU libraries ran on one `{python} gpu_name`, the GPU model used in @tbl-timing, with `{python} lib_release_text`, but each library's timing script ran separately from the benchmarks in @tbl-timing-full, so the Pypomp times in the two tables differ somewhat.
We left out Dynamax [@linderman25], since its only particle filter is a Rao--Blackwellized filter for switching linear Gaussian models.

@tbl-libraries gives two times for each GPU library: a call with the filter already compiled, and the first call, which includes JIT compilation.
IF2 compiles its filter once and then runs it at every iteration, so in an IF2 search with hundreds of iterations the compiled time dominates, and we compare the libraries by it below, against Pypomp with its default XLA backend.

On the cholera model, `pfjax` and `cuthbert` took `{python} fmt_range(lib_dacca_jax, 1)` times as long as Pypomp.
On the measles models, `pfjax` and `cuthbert` took `{python} fmt_range(lib_measles_jax, 0)` times as long as Pypomp for London, and neither finished its first call on the 4-town panel within an hour.
Most of this gap comes from the `jax.random` rejection samplers, which these libraries use for the binomial, gamma, and Poisson draws of the measles model (Appendix -@sec-samplers).
The PyTorch library `pydpf` took `{python} fmt_range(lib_pydpf, 1)` times as long as Pypomp on the cholera and measles models.
On the S&P 500 model, whose steps are cheap, every GPU library's first call took under two seconds, and `pydpf`'s first call, at `{python} f"{lib_s('spx', 'pydpf'):.2f}"` seconds, was slightly faster than Pypomp's `{python} f"{lib_s('spx', 'pypomp'):.2f}"` seconds.
Once compiled, Pypomp was the fastest GPU library on all four models, and its CuTe backend ran the compiled filter a further `{python} fmt_range(lib_cute_gain, 1)` times as fast as its default XLA backend.

The CPU-only libraries `particles` and `pypfilt` were timed on one core, and we scaled each time to 36 cores assuming perfect scaling, which flatters them.
Under this assumption, `particles` took `{python} f"{min(lib_cpu_vs_r['particles']):.1f}"` to `{python} f"{max(lib_cpu_vs_r['particles']):.1f}"` times the measured pomp time, and `pypfilt` took `{python} f"{min(lib_cpu_vs_r['pypfilt']):.1f}"` to `{python} f"{max(lib_cpu_vs_r['pypfilt']):.1f}"` times the pomp time.

::: {#tbl-libraries}
```{python}
#| echo: false


def fmt_lib_s(x):
    return f"{x:.2f}" if x < 1 else fmt_s(x)


def fmt_lib(model, column):
    """Compiled time, and the first call in parentheses, for one library."""
    row = lib_times.loc[(model, column)]
    if row["status"] == "timeout":  # never compiled, so no compiled time
        return "---", f"($>${row['first_s']:,.0f})"
    if column in CPU_LIBS:  # projected from CPU runs, with no compilation
        return fmt_s(row["first_s"]), ""
    return fmt_lib_s(row["warm_s"]), f"({fmt_lib_s(row['first_s'])})"


# Each model takes two rows: compiled times, then first calls in parentheses.
rows = []
for model, label in TIMING_MODELS.items():
    compiled, first = zip(
        *(fmt_lib(model, c) for c in ["pypomp", "pypomp_cute", *GPU_LIBS, *CPU_LIBS])
    )
    r = fmt_s(pf_time(timing[model]["R"]["times"]))
    rows.append(f"{label} & " + " & ".join(compiled) + f" & {r}")
    rows.append(" & " + " & ".join(first) + " & ")
tbl = latex_table(
    "lrrrrrrrr",
    [
        " & \\multicolumn{5}{c}{1 GPU} & \\multicolumn{3}{c}{36 CPU cores} \\\\",
        "\\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \\cmidrule(lr){7-9}",
        " & \\multicolumn{2}{c}{Pypomp} & & & & & & \\\\",
        "\\cmidrule(lr){2-3}",
        "Model & XLA & CuTe & \\texttt{pfjax} & \\texttt{cuthbert} & \\texttt{pydpf} "
        "& \\texttt{particles}$^\\dagger$ & \\texttt{pypfilt}$^\\dagger$ & \\texttt{pomp}$^*$ \\\\",
    ],
    rows,
)
# Nine columns fit the text width only with slightly tighter column spacing.
Markdown(tbl.data.replace("\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{4pt}", "\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2pt}"))
```

Wall-clock time in seconds for the particle filter benchmarks of @tbl-timing-full in Pypomp `{python} tbl_libraries_version` with its default XLA backend and with its CuTe backend and Philox generator, `pfjax` `{python} lib_version["pfjax"]` and `cuthbert` `{python} lib_version["cuthbert"]` (JAX), `pydpf` `{python} lib_version["pydpf"]` (PyTorch), and `particles` `{python} lib_version["particles"]` and `pypfilt` `{python} lib_version["pypfilt"]` (NumPy). GPU times are from one `{python} gpu_name`; for each model, the first row is the time for a call with the filter already compiled, and the second row, in parentheses, is the first call, which includes JIT compilation. ($>3{,}600$) means the first call did not finish within an hour, so there is no compiled time. For the measles models, `pfjax` and `cuthbert` draw with the `jax.random` samplers (Appendix -@sec-samplers). $^\dagger$`particles` and `pypfilt` run only on CPUs; their times are the time for one filter on one core, multiplied by the number of filters and divided by 36. $^*$`panelPomp` for the 4-town panel, as in @tbl-timing-full. `{python} version_warning("tbl-libraries")`
:::


# GPU scaling tests {#sec-scaling}

```{python}
#| label: scaling-plot-setup
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter, NullFormatter
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats

set_matplotlib_formats("pdf")  # vector output for the PDF manuscript

# Categorical slots 1 and 2 of the dataviz reference palette (validated for
# color-vision deficiency); marker shape is a second cue for grayscale print.
BLUE, ORANGE = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"
INK, MUTED, GRID = "#222222", "#6b6b6b", "#e4e4e0"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 8, "axes.edgecolor": MUTED, "axes.labelcolor": INK,
    "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "axes.linewidth": 0.6,
})


def log_axis(axis, ticks, lo, hi):
    """Log scale with plain-number labels at the given ticks between lo and hi."""
    axis.axes.set_xscale("log") if axis is axis.axes.xaxis else axis.axes.set_yscale("log")
    axis.set_ticks([t for t in ticks if lo <= t <= hi])
    axis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:,g}"))
    axis.set_minor_formatter(NullFormatter())
    (axis.axes.set_xlim if axis is axis.axes.xaxis else axis.axes.set_ylim)(lo, hi)


def bench_point(model):
    """Total IF2 particles (millions) and R cores matched in the @tbl-timing benchmark."""
    cores = R_CORES * timing[model]["R"]["times"]["mif"] / timing[model]["gpu"]["times"]["mif"]
    return bench_particles(model) / 1e6, cores


SCALING_TITLES = {
    "dacca": "Cholera, Dhaka",
    "measles": "Measles, London",
    "panel_measles": "Measles, 4-town panel",
    "spx": "S&P 500",
}


SCALING_KINDS = [  # how particles were added: color and marker shape
    ("chains", "More searches, 1,000 particles each", BLUE, "o"),
    ("particles", "More particles, fixed number of searches", ORANGE, "s"),
]
BACKENDS = [  # line style and marker fill: solid and filled for XLA, dashed and hollow for CuTe
    ("XLA (default)", scaling, "-", True),
    ("CuTe", scaling_cute, (0, (4, 2)), False),
]


def plot_scaling():
    from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.4), constrained_layout=True)
    for ax, model in zip(axes.flat, SCALING_MODELS):
        all_millions, top = [], 0
        for _, results, style, filled in BACKENDS:
            s = results[model]
            millions = s["total_particles_mif"] / 1e6
            all_millions.append(millions)
            top = max(top, s["r_cores"].max())
            for kind, _, color, marker in SCALING_KINDS:
                k = s["scaling_type"] == kind
                ax.plot(millions[k], s.loc[k, "r_cores"], color=color, marker=marker,
                        markersize=3.5, linewidth=1.3, linestyle=style,
                        markerfacecolor=color if filled else "white", markeredgewidth=1)
        millions = pd.concat(all_millions)
        bench_x, bench_y = bench_point(model)
        ax.plot(bench_x, bench_y, marker="D", markersize=4, color=INK, linestyle="none")
        log_axis(ax.xaxis, [0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30],
                 min(millions.min(), bench_x) / 1.3, millions.max() * 1.3)
        ax.set_ylim(0, max(top, bench_y) * 1.1)
        ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"{y:,.0f}"))
        ax.set_title(SCALING_TITLES[model], fontsize=8, color=INK, loc="left")
        ax.grid(True, color=GRID, linewidth=0.6)
        ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        for side in ("top", "right"):
            ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    for ax in axes[1]:
        ax.set_xlabel("Total particles (millions)")
    for ax in axes[:, 0]:
        ax.set_ylabel("R cores matched")
    # Two legend keys, read together: color and shape for how particles were
    # added, line style and fill for the backend. The legend fills column by
    # column, so each key gets its own column, then the benchmark.
    handles = [
        *(Line2D([], [], color=c, marker=mk, markersize=3.5, linewidth=1.3, label=lab)
          for _, lab, c, mk in SCALING_KINDS),
        *(Line2D([], [], color=MUTED, marker="o", markersize=3.5, linewidth=1.3, linestyle=st,
                 markerfacecolor=MUTED if filled else "white", label=lab)
          for lab, _, st, filled in BACKENDS),
        Line2D([], [], marker="D", markersize=4, color=INK, linestyle="none",
               label="Benchmark, XLA (Table 1)"),
    ]
    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="outside upper center", ncol=3, frameon=False)
    plt.show()


def best(model):
    return scaling[model].loc[scaling[model]["r_cores"].idxmax()]


scaling_m = sorted({int(s["M"].iloc[0]) for s in scaling.values()})
fixed_chains = sorted({
    int(s.loc[s["scaling_type"] == "particles", "chains"].iloc[0]) for s in scaling.values()
})
```

The benchmarks in @tbl-timing and @tbl-timing-full use the R configuration, which does not give the GPU enough work to reach its highest throughput for every model.
The scaling tests in quant ran IF2 on one `{python} gpu_name` GPU with more particles in flight, added in two ways: more searches of 1,000 particles each, or more particles for each of a fixed number of searches.
Each configuration, with $K$ searches of $J$ particles each ($KJ$ total particles in flight), ran in its own process and ran a short IF2 search of $m$ iterations twice, taking $t_{\mathrm{cold}}$ seconds on the first run and $t_{\mathrm{warm}}$ seconds on the second (excluding JIT compilation).
Projecting to the benchmark's $M$ IF2 iterations with compilation included gives the throughput, in particles filtered per second,
$$
\frac{K J M}{(t_{\mathrm{cold}} - t_{\mathrm{warm}}) + M \, t_{\mathrm{warm}} / m}.
$$
Each core in the pomp benchmark ran one search of $J_{\mathrm{R}}$ particles for $M$ iterations in $t_{\mathrm{R}}$ seconds, giving a single-core throughput of $J_{\mathrm{R}} M / t_{\mathrm{R}}$; dividing the GPU throughput by this rate gives the number of CPU cores running pomp that the GPU matches.
The highest value of this ratio over the scaling tests is the XLA Peak column of @tbl-timing, compared there and in @fig-scaling against the Cores column measured directly in the full-length timing benchmark, where $K = 36$, $J = J_{\mathrm{R}}$, and $t_{\mathrm{GPU}}$ includes compilation over all $M$ iterations without projection, reducing the ratio to $36 \, t_{\mathrm{R}} / t_{\mathrm{GPU}}$.
The scaling comparisons assume that pomp's time per particle per iteration does not depend on the number of particles or searches.

@fig-scaling shows the results.
With the default XLA backend, for every model, throughput peaks at between `{python} f"{min(best(m)['total_particles_mif'] for m in scaling) / 1e6:.1f}"` and `{python} f"{max(best(m)['total_particles_mif'] for m in scaling) / 1e6:.1f}"` million particles and falls or plateaus at larger sizes.
The peak is `{python} f"{peak_gain['dacca']:.1f}"` times the benchmark for the cholera model, `{python} f"{peak_gain['measles']:.1f}"` times for the London measles model, `{python} f"{peak_gain['panel_measles']:.1f}"` times for the 4-town panel, and `{python} f"{peak_gain['spx']:.1f}"` times for the S&P 500 model.
The S&P 500 model gains the most because its benchmark, with cheap steps and few particles, leaves the GPU mostly idle.
For this model, adding searches beats adding particles per search at a given total number of particles by an average of `{python} f"{(spx_chain_advantage - 1) * 100:.0f}"`%.
Consequently, there is not a large difference in speed between adding searches or particles per search on the GPU in terms of scaling with total particles.

The results above use JAX's default XLA compiler, which runs each Euler step of the process model as a sequence of GPU kernels that pass intermediate values through GPU memory.
Pypomp `{python} fig_scaling_version` also has an optional CuTe backend, which uses the CuTe DSL of NVIDIA's CUTLASS library [@thakkar23; @cecka26] to translate the process and measurement models into CUDA kernels that keep each particle's state on the chip between observations, and draws random numbers with Pypomp's implementation of the Philox4x32-10 generator of @salmon11.
We reran the same scaling tests with this backend, extended to as many as `{python} f"{max(s['total_particles_mif'].max() for s in scaling_cute.values()) / 1e6:.1f}"` million particles.
Its compilation takes longer, `{python} f"{cute_compile_s[0]:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{cute_compile_s[1]:.0f}"` seconds per configuration against `{python} f"{xla_compile_s[0]:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{xla_compile_s[1]:.0f}"` seconds for XLA, but its IF2 iterations are faster, and its highest throughput matches `{python} f"{min(peak_r_cores_cute.values()):,.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(peak_r_cores_cute.values()):,.0f}"` CPU cores running R, the CuTe peak column of @tbl-timing.
CuTe's throughput keeps rising to much larger sizes than XLA's (@fig-scaling).
For the S&P 500 model, it peaks at `{python} f"{spx_cute_peak_at['chains']:.1f}"` million particles when adding searches and `{python} f"{spx_cute_peak_at['particles']:.1f}"` million when adding particles per search, and then falls.
For the other models, it changed by less than `{python} f"{CUTE_TAIL:.0%}"` over the last doubling of particles, so larger configurations are unlikely to match many more cores.

With the CuTe backend, each million particles used about `{python} f"{vram_per_m['spx']:.0f}"` MB for the S&P 500 model, `{python} f"{vram_per_m['panel_measles']:.0f}"` MB for the 4-town panel, `{python} f"{vram_per_m['measles']:.0f}"` MB for the London measles model, and `{python} f"{vram_per_m['dacca']:.0f}"` MB for the cholera model, whether particles were added as searches or per search.
At the largest configurations it ran, the default XLA backend used about as much memory as CuTe.

::: {#fig-scaling}

```{python}
plot_scaling()
```

Blue adds searches of 1,000 particles each; orange adds particles to each of `{python} " or ".join(map(str, fixed_chains))` searches. Solid lines with filled markers use the default XLA backend of Pypomp `{python} fig_scaling_version`, and dashed lines with hollow markers use its CuTe backend. # Random variable samplers {#sec-samplers}

`jax.random` draws Poisson, binomial, and gamma random variables with rejection samplers, which loop a random number of times per draw.
This suits GPUs poorly, since threads that run together wait for the slowest one.
`pypomp.random` instead provides approximate inverse-CDF samplers, which avoid rejection loops.
@tbl-samplers compares the two on 1,000,000 draws per call, with parameters spread across the values where each sampler switches algorithms, averaged over 20 calls.
The approximation error is small: over a grid of parameter values, the Wasserstein distance between 1,000,000 draws from each `pypomp.random` sampler and from a reference sampler is at most `{python} f"{max_w1_norm * 100:.1f}"`% of the reference standard deviation.
In the London measles benchmark, the `jax.random` samplers made IF2 `{python} f"{jax_sampler_slowdown:.0f}"` times slower and particle filtering `{python} f"{jax_sampler_pf_slowdown:.0f}"` times slower on the GPU. `{python} version_warning("jax-samplers")`

::: {#tbl-samplers}
```{python}
#| echo: false
def fmt_ms(x):
    return "---" if x is None else (f"{x:,.0f}" if x >= 100 else f"{x:.2f}")


def ratio(num, den):
    return "---" if num is None else f"{num / den:.0f}$\\times$"


rows = []
for dist, (label, regime) in SAMPLER_ROWS.items():
    t = SAMPLERS[dist][regime]
    jax_gpu, jax_cpu = t.get("t_jax_gpu"), t.get("t_jax_cpu")
    w1 = max(SAMPLERS["grids"][dist]["w_dist_norm"])
    rows.append(
        f"{label} & {fmt_ms(t['t_pp_gpu'])} & {fmt_ms(jax_gpu)} & {ratio(jax_gpu, t['t_pp_gpu'])} "
        f"& {fmt_ms(t['t_pp_cpu'])} & {fmt_ms(jax_cpu)} & {ratio(jax_cpu, t['t_pp_cpu'])} & {w1:.3f}"
    )
latex_table(
    "lrrrrrrr",
    [
        "& \\multicolumn{3}{c}{GPU} & \\multicolumn{3}{c}{CPU} & \\\\",
        "\\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \\cmidrule(lr){5-7}",
        "Distribution & \\texttt{pypomp} & \\texttt{jax} & Ratio "
        "& \\texttt{pypomp} & \\texttt{jax} & Ratio & Max $W_1/\\sigma$ \\\\",
    ],
    rows,
)
```

Time in milliseconds for 1,000,000 draws from `pypomp.random` in Pypomp `{python} tbl_samplers_version` and `jax.random`, on one GPU and on one CPU core, with parameters spread across the values where the samplers switch algorithms. Ratio is the `jax.random` time divided by the `pypomp.random` time. `jax.random` has no negative binomial sampler. Max $W_1/\sigma$ is the largest Wasserstein distance between `pypomp.random` draws and draws from `jax.random` (or `scipy.stats` for the negative binomial) over a grid of parameter values, relative to the standard deviation. `{python} version_warning("tbl-samplers")`
:::

# England and Wales measles fit {#sec-big-measles-details}

We ran `{python} big_par["nreps_fitr"]` MPIF searches, each with `{python} f"{big_par['np_fitr']:,}"` particles for `{python} big_par["nfitr"]` iterations, and evaluated each endpoint with `{python} big_par["nreps_eval"]` particle filter replicates of `{python} f"{big_par['np_eval']:,}"` particles.
We then combined the best estimate for each town across searches and evaluated the result with another `{python} big_par["nreps_eval"]` replicates.
@tbl-big-measles gives the time for each stage on one GPU with Pypomp `{python} tbl_big_measles_version` and its CuTe backend.

For comparison, we estimated how long the same computation would take with panelPomp on a 36-core CPU node.
We measured panelPomp's cost per particle, per IF2 iteration, and per town on the 4-town panel in @tbl-timing-full, which covers the same period with the same daily time step, and scaled it linearly to the full computation.
We assume panelPomp fits the towns jointly with MPIF, as Pypomp did, so each search runs on one core and does not parallelize across units -- this would be necessary in the general case when using shared parameters.
By this estimate, R would need about `{python} r_big_months` months, `{python} big_speedup` times longer than the GPU with the CuTe backend, and about `{python} r_big_1core_years` years on a single core, so the GPU delivered the throughput of about `{python} big_core_ratio` CPU cores running R.
The wall clock time can be reduced further by spreading the searches over multiple GPUs.

::: {#tbl-big-measles}
```{python}
#| echo: false

def fmt_dur(s):
    if s >= 2 * DAY:
        return f"{s / DAY:.1f} days"
    if s >= 2 * HOUR:
        return f"{s / HOUR:.1f} hours"
    return f"{s / 60:.0f} minutes"


stages = [
    ("IF2", big_mif_s, r_big_mif_s),
    ("PF, all search endpoints", big_pf1_s, r_big_pf1_s),
    ("PF, combined estimate", big_pf2_s, r_big_pf2_s),
    ("\\textbf{Total}", big_total_s, r_big_total_s),
]
latex_table(
    "lrr",
    [
        " & Pypomp (1 GPU) & R \\texttt{panelPomp} \\\\",
        f"Stage & CuTe & 36 cores (estimated) \\\\",
    ],
    [f"{name} & {fmt_dur(g)} & {fmt_dur(r)}" for name, g, r in stages],
)
```
